docs.title: T1K
docs.text: T1K converts one JSON structure into another from a declarative mapping configuration, and converts the result back again. It is a Go package with a command-line tool, depends only on the Go standard library, and ships with the mapping that turns an EnerPlanET calculation payload into a MEME job.

docs.title: The core idea
docs.text:
A mapping configuration is a list of rules. Each rule pairs a path in the source document with a path in the target document, optionally passing the value through an invertible converter:

{"from": "order.total_cents", "to": "invoice.total", "convert": {"linear": {"divisor": 100}}}

The forward direction (Transform) reads the rule from from to to; the reverse direction (Reverse) reads it from to to from and runs the converter backwards. Every rule is written once and read in both directions, so one configuration yields both transformations and they cannot drift apart.

Paths may contain variables. A variable iterates on the side that is read and is substituted on the side that is written, which is how one rule moves a whole collection and restructures it:

{
  "each": {"from": "order.lines[$i]", "to": "invoice.items{line_$i}"},
  "rules": [
    {"from": "sku", "to": "article"},
    {"from": "qty", "to": "quantity", "convert": "number"}
  ]
}

This rule turns an array of lines into an object keyed line_0, line_1, ... and, in reverse, the object back into the array.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Installation and the Quickstart
  • Using the command line or the Go package
  • The mapping language: overview, paths and variables, rules, converters and the reverse direction
  • The shipped mapping: EnerPlanET to MEME
  • For contributors: architecture and testing

docs.title: Design goals
docs.text:
• Reversible by construction. A rule is a relation between two documents, not a procedure. Converters are invertible, and what cannot be inverted (a field the target has no place for) is restored from a declared default.
  • Strict configurations. Unknown keys, unbalanced variables, unknown converters and malformed conditions are rejected when a configuration is loaded, and every message names the position of the offending rule.
  • Faithful documents. A number keeps its digits unless a converter computes it; the input document is never modified; every conversion runs on its own state, so tasks can run in parallel.
  • No dependencies. The standard library only, so the package is easy to audit and to embed.

Status

T1K is pre-1.0. Before 1.0, a minor release may change the configuration format or the keys the shipped mapping generates; such changes are listed in the changelog with the keys concerned.

docs.title: Converters
docs.text:
A converter changes a value on its way from one side of a copy rule to the other. Every converter is invertible: the forward direction applies it forwards, the reverse direction backwards, and reverse(forward(v)) yields v again up to the documented loss of representation. A converter may also turn a value into absent, in which case the target key is not written and the rule's default for that direction, if any, applies.

convert takes one step or a list of steps applied in order; the reverse direction runs the list backwards. A step is a converter name, or an object with one key, the name, whose value holds the arguments:

"convert": "number"
"convert": {"linear": {"divisor": 1000}}
"convert": [{"absent": {"values": ["inf"], "ignore_case": true}}, {"linear": {"divisor": 1000}}]

Unknown converters and unknown or mistyped arguments are rejected when the configuration is loaded. An absent value passes through every converter unchanged.

Converter Forward Reverse identity the value as it is the same number a number or numeric string as a number the same string a scalar as a string a string that reads as a number or boolean back to one linear x * factor / divisor + offset solved for x lookup the right value of the pair whose left value matches the left value of the matching right value datetime a timestamp rendered in the to layout rendered in the from layout absent listed values become absent the same affix prefix + value + suffix the prefix and suffix stripped match the value, or an error when it does not match the pattern the same

docs.title: identity
docs.text: Passes the value through unchanged. It is the converter of a rule without convert; naming it explicitly is allowed.

docs.title: number
docs.text: Accepts a JSON number or a string holding one and yields a JSON number, in both directions. A number keeps its exact text (8.0 stays 8.0, 1e3 stays 1e3); a string is parsed and normalised (" 8 " becomes 8, "1e3" becomes 1000). Booleans, null, containers and strings that do not hold a finite decimal number are errors.

docs.title: string
docs.text: Forward renders a number or boolean as a string (8.5 to "8.5", true to "true"); strings pass through; null and containers are errors. Reverse turns a string that reads as a finite number or as true/false back into that value and leaves every other string alone; a non-string passes through.

docs.title: linear
docs.text:
y = x * factor / divisor + offset; the reverse solves for x.

Argument Default Meaning factor 1 multiplier divisor 1 divisor offset 0 added after scaling round_forward none round the forward result to this many decimals round_reverse none round the reverse result to this many decimals

factor and divisor must not be zero, and rounding decimals must not be negative. The input may be a number or a numeric string; anything else is an error. Results are emitted in plain decimal notation, rounded to 15 significant digits, so 8889.3 / 1000 is 8.8893 and never 8.889299999999999; a result that is not finite is an error.

Rounding is the one place a linear conversion loses information. The shipped mapping uses it to turn an annual energy in kWh into an average power in MW with nine decimals and back into whole kWh.

docs.title: lookup
docs.text:
Translates between two vocabularies through a list of pairs:

{"lookup": {"pairs": [[15, "15min"], [30, "30min"], [60, "1H"]], "strict": true}}

Forward maps the left value of a pair to its right value, reverse the right value to the left. Values are compared structurally (numbers by value, so 60.0 matches 60) and may be of any JSON type, objects and arrays included; the matched value is copied out of the table, never shared. Both columns must be free of duplicates so the table is invertible. A value without a pair is an error, or passes through unchanged when strict is false.

docs.title: datetime
docs.text:
Re-formats a timestamp string between two layouts:

{"datetime": {"from": "2006-01-02T15:04:05.000Z", "to": "RFC3339", "zone": "UTC"}}

Forward parses the value with from and renders it with to; reverse does the opposite. Both layouts are required. A layout is a Go reference layout, or one of the names RFC3339, RFC3339Nano, RFC1123, RFC1123Z, DateOnly (2006-01-02), DateTime (2006-01-02 15:04:05) and TimeOnly (15:04:05). Timestamps without zone information are read in zone, an IANA zone name that defaults to UTC, and output is rendered in that zone. A non-string value or a timestamp the layout cannot parse is an error.

Parts a layout does not carry (fractions of a second, the time of day with DateOnly) are lost on the way, which is the one place this converter is not exact.

docs.title: absent
docs.text:
Treats the listed values as not present, in both directions:

{"absent": {"values": ["inf", null], "ignore_case": true}}

With it, a placeholder such as "inf" or null is dropped instead of copied. Pair it with the rule's default or reverse_default to restore the placeholder in the other direction:

{"from": "cont_energy_cap_max", "to": "capacity.max",
 "convert": [{"absent": {"values": ["inf"]}}, {"linear": {"divisor": 1000}}],
 "reverse_default": "inf"}

values must be a non-empty list. Values compare structurally; ignore_case extends the match to strings that differ only in case and has no effect on other types.

docs.title: affix
docs.text:
Wraps a value in literal text:

{"affix": {"prefix": "n", "suffix": "", "strict": true}}

Forward renders prefix + value + suffix as a string; reverse strips both again. At least one of prefix and suffix is required. affix is the value-side counterpart of a key template such as {n$k}: where an identifier travels as a value rather than as a key, for example a node id copied into a reference, affix keeps it consistent with the wrapped key.

Forward accepts any scalar and always yields a string, so a number comes back from the reverse as the text of its digits; null and containers are errors. Reverse requires a string that starts with the prefix and ends with the suffix, and fails otherwise; with strict false such a value passes through unchanged. An empty value is wrapped and unwrapped like any other.

docs.title: match
docs.text:
A guard that changes nothing and fails when the value does not match a pattern:

{"match": {"pattern": "[^_\\d]\\w*"}}

The pattern uses Go regular expression syntax and is anchored to the whole value, so [a-z]+ and ^[a-z]+$ mean the same. The guard applies in both directions. Numbers and booleans are matched by their text; null and containers have no text and fail. An invalid pattern is rejected when the configuration is loaded.

Use match to turn a constraint of the target system, such as an identifier syntax, into an error that names the rule, instead of a rejection downstream. Chained after affix, it checks the wrapped value:

{"from": "from.id", "to": "from", "convert": [{"affix": {"prefix": "n"}}, {"match": {"pattern": "[^_\\d]\\w*"}}]}

docs.title: Mapping configuration
docs.text:
A mapping configuration is a JSON document that describes how one JSON structure maps onto another. T1K reads it in both directions: the forward direction builds the target document from the source document, the reverse direction builds the source document from the target document.

{
  "name": "enerplanet-to-meme",
  "version": "1.1.0",
  "description": "What the forward direction produces, in one or two sentences.",
  "definitions": {
    "costs": [ {"from": "cost_energy_cap", "to": "costs.monetary.investment_per_capacity"} ]
  },
  "rules": [
    {"from": "model_id", "to": "model.metadata.name"},
    {"each": {"from": "techs.pv", "to": "/model.technologies{pv_$k}"}, "rules": [ {"use": "costs"} ]}
  ]
}
Key Required Meaning name yes identifies the mapping; must not be empty version no the mapping's own version, free text description no what the forward direction produces definitions no named rule lists, spliced in wherever a rule says {"use": "name"} rules yes the rules, applied in order; may be empty $schema no accepted and ignored, for editors

Configurations are validated strictly when loaded. Any other key, at any level, is an error, as are unbalanced variables, unknown converters and malformed conditions, and every message names the position of the offending rule: rules[3].rules[1], or rules[2](definitions.costs)[0] for a rule spliced in from a definition.

The three kinds of rule are described on Rules, the path syntax on Paths and variables, the converters on Converters, and what all of this means when run backwards on The reverse direction.

docs.title: Evaluation model
docs.text:
Both directions follow the same procedure. The source is the input document and the target the document being built. In the forward direction a rule's from addresses the source and to the target; in the reverse direction the roles swap.

  1. The target starts as an empty object.
  2. Rules are applied in the order written. A copy rule reads the values its source path addresses, converts them, and writes them to the target path; a constant rule writes its value; an each rule applies its nested rules once per matched element.
  3. Writing creates the objects and arrays on the way. A value already present at the target path is replaced, so later rules win; a container of the wrong kind in the way is replaced as well.
  4. A copy rule whose source path addresses nothing writes nothing, unless it declares a default for that direction.
  5. After the last rule, arrays are compacted: positions no rule wrote (which arise when an index comes from a key such as item_5) are removed, so index variables need not be contiguous. Explicit null values are kept.

docs.title: Output conventions
docs.text:
• Numbers are carried as their original text. A value that is only moved keeps its digits (8.0 stays 8.0, 1e3 stays 1e3); a converter that computes a number emits it in plain decimal notation, rounded to 15 significant digits, so 8889.3 / 1000 is 8.8893.
  • Object keys are emitted in sorted order. JSON objects are unordered, and sorted output keeps results reproducible and diffs small.
  • The output never shares memory with the input: values are copied, never referenced.

docs.title: A complete example
docs.text:
{
  "name": "orders-to-invoices",
  "rules": [
    {"from": "order.number", "to": "invoice.reference"},
    {"from": "order.total_cents", "to": "invoice.total", "convert": {"linear": {"divisor": 100}}},
    {"to": "invoice.currency", "value": "EUR"},
    {"from": "order.status", "value": "converted"},
    {
      "each": {"from": "order.lines[$i]", "to": "invoice.items{line_$i}"},
      "when": {"forward": {"path": "qty", "gt": 0}},
      "rules": [
        {"from": "sku", "to": "article"},
        {"from": "qty", "to": "quantity", "convert": "number"},
        {"to": "position", "template": "$i"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Forward: the reference and the total are copied (the total divided by 100), the currency is set, and every line with a positive quantity becomes an item keyed by its position. Reverse: the reference and the total come back (the total multiplied by 100), the status is set to converted, and every line_N item becomes the line at position N. currency and position were written for the invoice side only and are simply not read.

docs.title: Paths and variables
docs.text:
A path addresses values in a JSON document. Every rule has one path per side, and each rules, bind entries and conditions use paths as well.

Syntax Addresses a.b.c object keys, separated by dots a[3] the element at a fixed array index a[$i] every array element, binding its index to $i a{$k} every entry of an object, binding its key to $k a{line_$i} every entry whose key fits the template, binding the variable part a{${p}_$i} a template with several variables, separated by literal text a[*], a{*} anonymous variables, named $_1, $_2, ... by position /a.b absolute: from the document root, even inside an each . the current element itself / the document root itself "my.key".x a quoted key may contain any character; \" and \\ escape

Suffixes chain and combine with keys: grid{$r}[$c] reads row $r, column $c; a[0]{$k} reads the entries of the first element. A segment that consists of suffixes alone, such as [0].x or {$k}.v, is allowed only at the start of a path, where it addresses the current element's own elements or entries. Whitespace around the expression is ignored; a bare key must not contain $, ., brackets or quotes (quote it instead).

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
A variable is $ followed by a name matching [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*, or ${name} where the name would otherwise run into following text ({${p}_$i}). A variable's value is always a string: an array index becomes "0", "1", ...; an object key is taken as it is.

Variables make rules bidirectional:

  • On the side being read, an unbound variable iterates: the rule applies once per element or entry that matches, and each match binds the variable.
  • On the side being written, every variable must be bound; its value is substituted into the path. A variable used as an array index must then hold a non-negative integer (leading zeros are accepted); anything else fails the rule.
  • A variable that is already bound, by an enclosing each or by an earlier step of the same path, selects exactly one element or entry.

A copy rule must therefore use the same variables on both sides, apart from those bound by an enclosing each:

{"from": "items[$i].v", "to": "byIndex{item_$i}.value"}

Forward, $i iterates the array and names the keys. Reverse, $i is parsed out of every item_N key and places the value at index N; keys that do not fit the template (other) are ignored.

docs.title: Anonymous variables
docs.text: [*] and {*} are named $_1, $_2, ... in order of appearance on each side of a rule, so items[*].name paired with things[*].label pairs the first * of one side with the first of the other. They are convenient for simple copies; use named variables as soon as a path has more than one, or a nested rule needs to refer to it.

docs.title: Key templates
docs.text:
The text between braces is a template of literal characters and variables. $$ stands for a literal dollar sign. A template without variables is a literal key: a{fixed} is the same as a.fixed.

A key is parsed by matching the template's literal text, so two variables must be separated by literal text: {$a$b} is rejected, {$a-$b} is accepted. Earlier variables take the shortest possible match and the last one takes the rest: for {${p}_$i}, the key lv_0 binds p=lv and i=0, and a_b_c binds p=a and i=b_c. A variable matches any characters, including newlines. Template text must be valid UTF-8; a template that is not is rejected when the configuration is loaded.

docs.title: Matching and absence
docs.text:
A path with no unbound variables addresses exactly one value, which is either present or absent. Absence is not an error: a copy rule with an absent source writes nothing (or its default), and a condition can test for it with exists. Reading through a value of the wrong kind (a key on an array, an index on an object, anything on a scalar) is likewise absence, as is an index beyond the end of an array.

A path with unbound variables yields one match per element or entry that exists, and none when nothing does.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text: Writing resolves a path to a concrete location, substituting every variable, and creates the objects and arrays on the way. Writing an index beyond the end of an array grows the array; the positions skipped are removed when the run completes (see the evaluation model). Writing to . or / replaces the current element or the whole output document with the value.

docs.title: The reverse direction
docs.text: Reverse is not a second mapping: it is the same rules read from to to from. This page collects what that means for each construct and how to write a mapping whose reverse does what you expect.

docs.title: What the reverse direction does with each construct
docs.text: Construct Forward direction Reverse direction copy rule read from, convert, write to read to, convert backwards, write from default written when from is absent ignored reverse_default ignored written when to is absent constant with to written ignored constant with from ignored written each enumerate the from elements, write below to enumerate the to entries, write below from, or join (see below) bind read the variable from the source element write the variable back to its path (iterate mode), or read it from the element earlier rules created (join mode) when.forward gates the rule ignored when.reverse ignored gates the rule converter chain steps in order steps backwards, each reversed

docs.title: Lossless and lossy
docs.text:
A copy rule with an invertible converter is lossless: the value comes back exactly, numbers to their digits unless a converter computed them. Three things are lossy by nature:

  • A source field with no counterpart on the target side is not carried. Declare what the reverse should put there with a from constant or a reverse_default, choose a value that is honest about being a placeholder, and document it.
  • A converter that rounds, or a datetime layout that drops parts, loses the digits or parts it does not keep.
  • A value whose type the target cannot express comes back in the type the target has: a number wrapped by affix, or bound to a variable and written back in iterate mode, returns as a string.

Everything else round-trips, and the shipped mapping's tests check exactly that: converting the reverse output forward again reproduces the job, and reversing that reproduces the reverse output.

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
Wrapped identifiers. A key template wraps a key (model.nodes{n$k}); the affix converter does the same for the value that references it and strips the text again in reverse, so a prefix that makes an id valid for the target never leaks back into the source. A match guard behind it reports an id the prefix cannot repair:

{"from": "from.id", "to": "from", "convert": [{"affix": {"prefix": "n"}}, {"match": {"pattern": "[^_\\d]\\w*"}}]}

Placeholder values. EnerPlanET's "inf" means "no bound" and has no MEME counterpart. Drop it forward with absent, restore it backwards with reverse_default:

{"from": "cont_energy_cap_max", "to": "capacity.max",
 "convert": [{"absent": {"values": ["inf"], "ignore_case": true}}, {"linear": {"divisor": 1000}}],
 "reverse_default": "inf"}

Defaults before values. A from constant followed by a copy rule for the same path gives "this value, unless the target has a real one":

{"from": "properties.demand_energy", "value": 0},
{"each": {"from": "properties", "to": "/model.technologies{demand_$k}"},
 "rules": [{"from": "demand_energy", "to": "demand_profile", "convert": {"linear": {"divisor": 8760000}}}]}

Discriminators. A source field that selects a shape (feature_type being BasePOI or TopologyNode) can often be reconstructed from what the forward direction produced for each shape. Two from constants with complementary when.reverse conditions do it:

{"from": "properties.feature_type", "value": "BasePOI",      "when": {"reverse": {"path": "/model.trade{grid_$k}", "exists": false}}},
{"from": "properties.feature_type", "value": "TopologyNode", "when": {"reverse": {"path": "/model.trade{grid_$k}", "exists": true}}}

Collections keyed by value. An each with bind whose key does not carry the array position runs in join mode backwards: it fills the elements that earlier rules created. Order the rules so that the creating rule (the one that writes topology[$i] with from.id) comes first. Elements nothing creates are not restored; in the shipped mapping that is a building without a connection, which has a node but no transmission arc.

Keys that carry positions. A template such as {line_$i} paired with topology[$i] places entries by the number in their key. Entries whose key does not fit the template are skipped; a key that fits but holds something other than a non-negative integer is an error, because it cannot be an index. Gaps in the numbers are closed when arrays are compacted at the end.

docs.title: Checking a mapping
docs.text: For any mapping, the useful checks are: Reverse(Transform(x)) has the shape of x with only the declared placeholders differing; Transform(Reverse(Transform(x))) equals Transform(x); and both outputs are accepted by the systems that will read them. Testing describes how the repository does this for the shipped mapping.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
rules is a list. Every entry is one of three kinds of rule (copy, constant or each), or a use of a definition. Rules apply in the order written, and a later write to a path replaces an earlier one.

Kind Recognised by Purpose copy from and to, no value or template move a value between the two sides, optionally converted constant value or template write a fixed value on one side each each apply nested rules to every element of a collection use use splice a named rule list from definitions

Every rule accepts description, free text that T1K ignores.

docs.title: Copy rules
docs.text:
{"from": "cont_energy_cap_max", "to": "capacity.max",
 "convert": [{"absent": {"values": ["inf"]}}, {"linear": {"divisor": 1000}}],
 "reverse_default": "inf",
 "description": "kW to MW; 'inf' means unbounded"}
Key Meaning from the path on the source side: read by the forward direction, written by the reverse to the path on the target side: written by the forward direction, read by the reverse convert a converter or a list of them, applied in order; the reverse direction runs them backwards default written to to by the forward direction when from is absent, or the converter made the value absent reverse_default written to from by the reverse direction when to is absent when conditions per direction

from and to must use the same variables, apart from those an enclosing each binds. A default applies only when the path is concrete (no unbound variables), because the absence of an iterated path is simply zero matches.

The value at the source path is copied as a whole: an object or array moves with everything inside it, and nothing is taken by reference.

docs.title: Constant rules
docs.text:
{"to": "experiment.mode", "value": "plan"}
{"from": "geometry.type", "value": "Point"}
{"to": "node", "template": "n$k"}

A constant has exactly one side. A constant with to is written by the forward direction, one with from by the reverse direction; the other direction ignores the rule. value may be any JSON value, including null, objects and arrays; template is a string in which $k, ${k} and $$ are substituted from the enclosing each bindings. A constant's path may use only variables an enclosing each binds.

Constants are how the reverse direction restores what the forward direction cannot carry: declare the value a source field should have when its target counterpart does not exist. Place such a constant before the copy rule for the same path, so a real value, when present, wins.

docs.title: Each rules
docs.text:
{
  "each": {"from": "topology[$i].from", "to": "model.nodes{n$k}", "bind": {"$k": "id"}},
  "when": {"forward": {"path": "properties.feature_type", "equals": "BasePOI"}},
  "rules": [
    {"from": "geometry.coordinates[1]", "to": "coords.lat", "convert": "number"},
    {"from": "properties.osm_id", "to": "name"},
    {"from": "properties.demand_energy", "to": "/model.technologies{demand_$k}.demand_profile"}
  ]
}
Key Meaning each.from the path of the source elements each.to the path of the target elements each.bind variables read from values inside each source element (see bind) rules the rules applied to every pair of elements, with paths relative to the pair; may be omitted or empty when conditions, evaluated per element

Inside the nested rules, relative paths start at the current element on each side; absolute paths (/...) start at the document root. The variables bound by the each, and by enclosing ones, are available in nested paths, templates and conditions.

In the forward direction the elements of each.from are enumerated in the source document and the nested rules write below each.to; in the reverse direction the entries of each.to are enumerated and the nested rules write below each.from. An each whose paths have no variables applies its rules once if the element exists and not at all otherwise, which makes it the way to write a group of constants only when a source object is present.

docs.title: bind
docs.text:
bind maps variables to paths read from each source element:

"bind": {"$k": "id"}

The value at the path must be a string, number or boolean and becomes the variable's binding, as text; a missing or non-scalar value fails the rule, so a mapping never drops elements silently. A bind variable must be new (not bound by an enclosing each nor by each.from), must appear in each.to, and its path may use the variables the iteration binds.

With bind, the target side can be keyed by a value instead of a position: topology[$i].from paired with model.nodes{n$k} and {"$k": "id"} turns an array of features into an object keyed by their ids, and writes a feature that appears several times only once.

How the reverse direction enumerates depends on whether each.to determines every variable of each.from:

  • Iterate mode, when it does (conns[$i] with arcs{${p}_$i} and {"$p": "pipe"}): the target entries are enumerated, each key is parsed, and every bound variable is written back to its bind path as a string (pipe gets "lv").
  • Join mode, when it does not (topology[$i].from with model.nodes{n$k}: $i is not in the key): the each looks at the source elements that earlier rules have already created in the output, reads the bind path from each of them (id), and fills the element from the matching target entry. Such a rule must therefore come after the rules that create those elements and their bind values; entries without a created element are not restored.

docs.title: Nesting
docs.text:
each rules nest. A nested each may address its own collections relative to the current element or, with absolute paths, elsewhere in the document, which is how per-element technologies are collected into one top-level map:

{"each": {"from": "techs.pv_supply", "to": "/model.technologies{pv_supply_$k}"}, "rules": [...]}

docs.title: Definitions and use
docs.text: definitions holds named rule lists; {"use": "name"} splices one in place. The spliced rules are compiled where they are used, so they may rely on the variables bound at that place (a definition used inside an each over model.nodes{n$k} may use $k), and one definition can serve several each rules. A definition may use other definitions; cycles are rejected.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
"when": {
  "forward": [{"path": "feature_type", "equals": "TopologyNode"}, {"path": "rated_power", "gt": 0}],
  "reverse": {"path": "/model.trade{grid_$k}", "exists": true}
}

when gates a rule per direction: forward applies to the forward direction, reverse to the reverse direction, and a direction without conditions always applies. Each direction takes one condition or a list of conditions, all of which must hold. A condition names a path, evaluated against the source document of that direction, relative to the current element (for an each, the element itself) or absolute with /. The path may use bound variables and must address a single value. Its remaining keys are operators, all of which must hold:

Operator Holds when exists: true / false the path is present / absent equals: v the value is present and equals v (structurally; numbers by value) not_equals: v the value is absent or differs from v in: [v, ...] the value is present and equals one of the list gt, gte, lt, lte: n the value is a number in the given relation to n; a non-number never holds

The forward conditions of an each run before its bind paths are read, so they may use the iteration variables but not the bound ones; reverse conditions have every variable bound.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
T1K is a small Go module with one public package and four internal ones, each with a single responsibility. It depends only on the standard library.

pkg/t1k              the public API: TransformTask, Config, errors
config               the shipped mapping files, embedded
cmd/t1k              the command line
internal/mapping     the mapping language: compiling rules, evaluating them
internal/jsonpath    path expressions: parsing, matching, locations
internal/convert     the invertible value converters
internal/jsondoc     the JSON document model every layer works on

pkg/ follows the layout of the organisation's shared Go libraries; the Go team's own layout guide would also accept the package at the module root.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
Package Responsibility Depends on pkg/t1k TransformTask with Transform and Reverse, Config loading, the default configuration parsed at initialisation, the error sentinels mapping, jsondoc, config config the mapping files under config/, embedded with go:embed and named nothing internal/mapping Compile turns a configuration into a Program of rules; Program.Run applies them in a Direction jsonpath, convert, jsondoc internal/jsonpath Parse reads a path expression; Expand matches it against a document, binding variables; Resolve, Get and Set work with concrete locations; Compact removes the holes out-of-order writes leave jsondoc (tests only) internal/convert Parse builds a Converter from a rule's convert; each converter implements Forward and Reverse jsondoc internal/jsondoc Decode and Encode with numbers kept as json.Number, DeepCopy, structural Equal, number parsing and formatting, type names for messages nothing cmd/t1k flags, files and exit codes around the public API pkg/t1k

Dependencies point downwards only. The public package knows nothing about paths or converters; the mapping package knows nothing about files or formatting.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
input bytes ──jsondoc.Decode──▶ tree ──Program.Run(direction)──▶ tree ──jsondoc.Encode──▶ output bytes

Decode keeps numbers as json.Number, so a value that is only moved is emitted with its original digits. Run creates a run per call with the direction, the input tree and an output tree that starts as an empty object; nothing is shared between calls, which is why a task can be used concurrently.

docs.title: Compilation
docs.text:
mapping.Compile parses the JSON into a tree of rule values (rule.go) of three kinds: copy, constant and scope (each). One file compiles each kind (compile.go for the document, definitions, copy and constant rules, compile_scope.go for scopes and their bind, condition.go for when), reading raw JSON through the fields helper (fields.go) so every mistake is reported with the field's name and the rule's position. Compilation resolves every path, key template, converter chain and condition once and checks the variable discipline that makes rules reversible:

  • a copy rule uses the same unbound variables on both sides;
  • a constant or template uses only variables an enclosing each binds;
  • an each binds every variable of to through from or bind, and records whether the reverse must join (some variable of from is not in to) or can iterate.

use splices a definition's rules at the use site and compiles them there, so a definition sees the variables bound where it is used; cycles are detected with a stack of open definitions.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
A frame is where the rules currently apply: the bindings, the input element relative paths read from, and the output Location relative paths write to. The root frame has no bindings, the whole input and the root location.

The direction only decides which side of a rule is read and which is written, which converter direction runs, which default and which conditions apply, and which of a scope's two modes runs backwards (run.go holds the copy and constant rules, run_scope.go the scopes). Reading uses Path.Expand, which walks the tree with the current bindings, iterating unbound variables and selecting with bound ones, and returns one Match per addressed value; a concrete path returns one match, present or not, so a rule can tell absence from "nothing matched". Writing uses Path.Resolve, which substitutes every variable into a concrete location, and Set, which creates containers on the way and grows arrays with holes that Compact removes at the end.

docs.title: Converters
docs.text: A converter implements Forward and Reverse over a (value, present) pair, so it can turn a value into absence and back. A chain runs its steps in order forward and backwards in reverse. The scalar converters (identity, number, string) share scalar.go; every other converter (linear, lookup, datetime, absent, affix, match) has a file of its own. Factories read their arguments through a strict reader (args.go) that rejects unknown ones, so a misspelt argument fails at load time.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• Bidirectional by construction: there is one rule set and one engine; nothing is written twice.
  • Strict at load, tolerant at run: a configuration error is reported before any document is touched; an absent value at run time is not an error, a value of the wrong type for a converter is.
  • Faithful documents: numbers keep their text, the input is never modified, the output never aliases the input.
  • Deterministic output: sorted keys, computed numbers in plain decimal notation, stable compaction.
  • Small functions: every function does one thing and says so in its comment; the engine is a set of named steps, not one loop.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
make test        # go test ./...
make test-race   # go test -race -shuffle=on ./...
make lint        # go vet + golangci-lint (v2, configuration in .golangci.yml)
make cover       # coverage summary
make fuzz        # every fuzz target, FUZZTIME each (default 30s)
make bench       # benchmarks of Transform and Reverse on the example

CI runs lint, the race tests, a build, a conversion of the example in both directions, a ten-second fuzz smoke of every target and govulncheck on every push and pull request, and it builds the containerized environment and runs the race tests and lint inside it.

docs.title: In a container
docs.text:
environment/ provides the same targets inside a Docker image with the toolchain CI uses (see the folder's README):

make -C environment build            # one-time image build
make -C environment test  ENV=dev    # go test ./..., with Go's caches
make -C environment check ENV=test   # race tests and lint, no test cache

docs.title: Layers
docs.text: Tests What they pin internal/jsondoc/jsondoc_test.go decoding with exact digits, encoding (and what cannot be encoded), deep copies, structural equality, Go and JSON numbers, non-finite text, number formatting at the edges, type names internal/jsonpath/path_test.go parsing of every path form and its error messages, the String() round trip, key template matching and rendering, matching with bound and unbound variables (leading zeros, out-of-range and non-integer bindings, errors inside iterations), concrete locations, reads and writes through holes and wrong containers, compaction internal/convert/convert_test.go every converter forward and back (each case is run both ways), argument and type validation, absent inputs, chains and their error propagation, zone rendering, non-finite text, structural lookups internal/mapping/compile_test.go a valid configuration with every construct, unusual but valid shapes, bind ordering and join detection, and one case per validation error with the message and the rule position it must produce internal/mapping/run_test.go table cases for copy rules, constants and templates, arrays and keyed objects, each in iterate and join mode, nested scopes, every condition operator, defaults, roots and nulls, and every runtime error path with its rule position and direction; each case checks forward and reverse pkg/t1k/t1k_test.go, pkg/t1k/config_test.go the public API, golden files for the default mapping, the round-trip property, the concurrency guarantee, error classification pkg/t1k/calliope_test.go the regression test for issue #1: every generated key and reference satisfies Calliope's identifier syntax, every reference resolves, the reverse restores EnerPlanET's ids, and an id the prefix cannot repair fails with the rule named pkg/t1k/mapping_test.go the default mapping's behaviour for every technology kind, payload edge cases (no topology, standalone buildings, zero demand and rating, resolutions, infinity spellings), values it must reject, the reverse of jobs T1K did not produce, the round trip over a payload with every kind, and degenerate inputs config/config_test.go the default mapping is embedded and is JSON cmd/t1k/main_test.go flags, files, standard streams, exit codes and error messages

docs.title: Fuzzing
docs.text: Every parser and the transformation itself have a fuzz target next to their tests: FuzzParse and FuzzParseTemplate in jsonpath (no expression panics, accepted ones round-trip through String(), rendered keys match their template), FuzzParse in convert (no spec panics, parsed converters survive representative inputs in both directions) and FuzzAffix (the affix round trip holds for arbitrary prefixes, suffixes and values), FuzzCompile and FuzzRun in mapping (no configuration or document panics, every failure wraps ErrConfig or ErrRule) and FuzzTransform in pkg/t1k (the default mapping never panics on any input in either direction). go test runs their seed corpora; make fuzz explores for FUZZTIME per target and CI runs a short smoke. A crasher lands in testdata/fuzz/ of the package; commit it as a regression case once fixed.

docs.title: Golden files
docs.text:
pkg/t1k/testdata/meme-job.golden.json and pkg/t1k/testdata/enerplanet-reverse.golden.json are the outputs of the default mapping for examples/enerplanet-calculation.json in both directions. After a deliberate change to the mapping:

make golden-update
git diff pkg/t1k/testdata

Review every changed line; the diff is the change's effect on the contract.

docs.title: The round-trip property
docs.text: TestDefaultMappingRoundTrip converts the example forward, back and forward again and requires the second job to equal the first apart from the building without a connection, which the reverse cannot place (see the mapping page). It then reverses the second job and requires that output to equal the first reverse output, so the transformation is stable from the first round trip on. A new lossy rule shows up here immediately.

docs.title: Checking against the consumers
docs.text:
MEME's decoder rejects unknown fields and its validators check the model, so the surest test of a mapping change is MEME itself. In a clone of the MEME repository, a small program in cmd/ can decode a job with json.Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields, call job.Model.Validate() and job.Experiment.Validate(), and run each registered target's ValidateJob to see the per-target gates and warnings; the compatibility table on the mapping page was produced that way.

The reverse output can be checked against the simulation engine's servicehub/schemas/calliope.json with any JSON Schema validator. It passes once the placeholders the mapping documents (country, ...) are filled in.

docs.title: Branch Naming Convention
docs.text:
All repositories follow the Conventional Branch specification, extended with additional types to mirror the commit convention.

Branch names are automatically validated when a pull request is opened. A PR cannot be merged until the branch name passes the check.

docs.title: Format
docs.text: <type>/<description>

docs.title: Types
docs.text: Type Purpose feat/ or feature/ New feature fix/ or bugfix/ Bug fix hotfix/ Urgent production fix (branches off main) release/ Release preparation chore/ Tooling, dependencies, CI changes docs/ Documentation only refactor/ Code restructuring, no behaviour change test/ Tests only style/ Formatting, whitespace — no logic changes perf/ Performance improvements

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Lowercase only — no uppercase letters
  • Hyphens as separators — no underscores, no spaces
  • No consecutive hyphens or dots — -- and .. are not allowed
  • No leading or trailing hyphens or dots
  • Dots only for version numbers — e.g. release/v1.2.0
  • Ticket numbers are allowed — e.g. feat/issue-123-login-page

docs.title: Exempt branches
docs.text:
The following branches are exempt from naming rules:

main, master, dev, develop, staging

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
feat/add-geospatial-query
fix/token-expiry-validation
hotfix/critical-data-loss
docs/update-api-reference
chore/upgrade-dependencies
release/v2.1.0
refactor/simplify-coordinate-transform
test/add-export-unit-tests
feat/issue-42-user-authentication

docs.title: Invalid examples
docs.text: Branch name Problem Feature/AddLogin Uppercase letters fix/header_bug Underscore — use fix/header-bug new-feature Missing type prefix feat/new--login Consecutive hyphens fix/ Empty description

docs.title: GitHub auto-generated branch names
docs.text:
When you create a branch directly from a GitHub issue using the "Create a branch" button, GitHub generates a name like 123-fix-login-bug. This format has no type prefix and will fail the check.

Rename it before opening a PR:

git fetch origin
git checkout 123-fix-login-bug
git branch -m 123-fix-login-bug fix/123-login-bug
git push origin -u fix/123-login-bug
git push origin --delete 123-fix-login-bug

docs.title: Fixing a failed branch name check
docs.text:
The branch name check only runs when the PR is opened or reopened. To fix a failing branch name you need to rename the branch and update the PR.

# Rename the branch locally
git branch -m old-branch-name feat/correct-branch-name

# Push the renamed branch and update remote tracking
git push origin -u feat/correct-branch-name

# Delete the old branch from remote
git push origin --delete old-branch-name

Then update the PR base branch on GitHub if needed, or close and reopen the PR from the renamed branch.

docs.title: Commit Message Conventions
docs.text:
All repositories in the THD-Spatial-AI and enerplanet organizations follow the Conventional Commits specification, originally adopted by the EU Commission component library.

Commit messages are automatically validated on every pull request. A PR cannot be merged until all commit messages pass the check.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
<type>(<scope>): <subject>

<body>

<footer>

Only the first line is required. Body and footer are optional.

docs.title: Types
docs.text: Type When to use feat A new feature fix A bug fix docs Documentation changes only style Formatting or whitespace — no logic changes refactor Code restructuring without new features or bug fixes perf Performance improvements test Adding or updating tests chore Build process, tooling, or dependency updates

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Use imperative mood — write add login endpoint, not added login endpoint
  • No capital letter at the start of the subject
  • No period at the end of the subject
  • Max 100 characters per line
  • Scope is optional but recommended — use it to indicate the affected area (e.g. api, auth, docs)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
feat(api): add geospatial query endpoint
fix(auth): correct token expiry validation
docs: update installation instructions
chore(ci): upgrade actions/checkout to v4
refactor(parser): simplify coordinate transformation logic
test(export): add unit tests for GeoJSON output

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
Add a BREAKING CHANGE: footer when a change is not backwards compatible:

feat(api): replace coordinate system

BREAKING CHANGE: all endpoints now return WGS84 instead of ETRS89

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Wrong Correct updated readme docs: update readme Fix bug fix: correct null pointer in parser feat: Add new endpoint. feat: add new endpoint WIP chore: scaffold route handler

docs.title: Fixing a failed commit lint check
docs.text: When the Validate commit messages check fails on your PR, follow the steps below depending on how many commits need fixing.

docs.title: Fix the most recent commit
docs.text:
git commit --amend -m "feat(scope): your corrected message"
git push --force-with-lease

docs.title: Fix multiple commits
docs.text:
Use an interactive rebase to reword each failing commit. The workflow log tells you exactly which commit SHAs need fixing.

# Replace N with the number of commits in your PR
git rebase -i HEAD~N

In the editor that opens, change pick to reword for each commit you want to fix, save and close. Git will pause at each one so you can enter the corrected message. Then push:

git push --force-with-lease

docs.title: Using AI to rewrite messages
docs.text:
If you are unsure how to rewrite a message, paste it into an AI assistant:

"My commit message update greeting message in main function failed the conventional commits check. The allowed types are: feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, chore. Please rewrite it in the correct format type(scope): subject."

The AI will suggest something like feat(main): update greeting message.

Force push requires branch to be up to date

After --force-with-lease, the PR will automatically re-run the commit lint check. If someone else pushed to the branch in the meantime, the force push will be rejected — pull first with git pull --rebase and then push again.

docs.title: EnerPlanET to MEME
docs.text: config/enerplanet-to-meme.json, the mapping embedded in the package, converts the calculation payload EnerPlanET's backend sends to its simulation webservice into a MEME job, the body of MEME's POST /simulate. This page records what it maps, the decisions behind it and what the reverse direction restores.

docs.title: The two documents
docs.text:
Source: the CalculationPayload built by enerplanet/backend/internal/payload/payload.go. Its topology is an array of connections; each connection has a from feature, and, unless the building stands alone, a to feature, a length in km and a pipe kind (lv building to transformer, mv transformer to transformer). A feature is a GeoJSON point with properties (identity, usage class, annual demands) and a techs object keyed by the technology catalogue (pv_supply, battery_storage, ...) whose entries hold Calliope 0.6 constraint names in kW, kWh and EUR/kW. The simulation engine's servicehub/schemas/calliope.json describes the shape.

Target: MEME's canonical model (internal/model in the MEME repository): nodes, technologies, transmission and trade keyed by identifiers, quantities in MW, MWh and EUR/MW, plus an experiment. MEME decodes the body with unknown fields disallowed, so the job may contain nothing MEME does not define.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• A node per feature, an arc per connection. Every building and transformer becomes a node keyed by its feature id with the prefix n (n1, ntrafo_2585); every connection becomes a bidirectional transmission arc keyed by pipe kind and position (lv_0, mv_2) with the length as distance. The topology is therefore preserved exactly and the reverse can rebuild it. (The translator on EnerPlanET's feature/heat-integration branch instead sums buildings into one node per transformer area; that aggregation cannot be inverted, so T1K keeps the features.)
  • Identifiers that Calliope accepts. Calliope 0.7 requires identifiers to match ^[^_^\d][\w]*$: no leading digit or underscore, and only letters, digits and _. EnerPlanET numbers its buildings, so node ids get the prefix n, and every generated key joins its parts with _ (demand_1, pv_supply_1, grid_trafo_2585, households_1). The node references copied into transmission arcs get the same prefix through the affix converter and are checked by a match guard, so an id that cannot be made valid fails the transformation rather than MEME's Calliope target. The reverse strips the prefix, so EnerPlanET's ids come back unchanged. This answers issue #1.
  • The transformer is the grid connection. As in the simulation engine, which attaches a transformer_supply technology capped by the rated power, each transformer gets a trade entry importing at most its rating (kVA as MW) at 300 EUR/MWh, the tariff of that template technology, with unpaid export. households_supply and non_households_supply attached to a building become a trade at the building with their own tariff.
  • kW to MW, divided by 1000, for capacities, storage sizes and the transformer rating; EUR/kW, EUR/kWh and EUR/kW/a are multiplied by 1000.
  • Annual demand as average power. demand_energy (kWh/a) becomes a constant demand_profile in MW (divided by 8760 h and 1000), rounded to nine decimals; the reverse rounds back to whole kWh. A time series can be put in its place by pointing the rule at model.timeseries.
  • Run settings from the Calliope template: mode plan, objective min_cost, solver highs, unmet demand allowed at a penalty of 1e6 EUR/MWh (ensure_feasibility with bigM: 1e6).
  • Electricity only. Heat demand (demand_heat) is carried by no rule; the reverse writes 0.

docs.title: Identifiers
docs.text:
MEME accepts letters, digits, ., _ and - in identifiers, but its Calliope target applies Calliope's stricter rule, ^[^_^\d][\w]*$. The mapping therefore generates every key and reference as follows:

EnerPlanET MEME key MEME references building id 1 node n1 node: "n1" in its technologies and trades; from/to: "n1" in arcs transformer id trafo_2585 node ntrafo_2585 node: "ntrafo_2585" in its trade; from/to in arcs demand of building 1 technology demand_1 techs.pv_supply of building 1 technology pv_supply_1 techs.households_supply of building 1 trade households_1 transformer trafo_2585 rating trade grid_trafo_2585 connection at position 0 with pipe lv arc lv_0

The prefix comes from the key template model.nodes{n$k} and the templates n$k of the node references; the references copied from the topology (from.id, to.id) get it through the affix converter followed by a match guard. An id that is still invalid after the prefix, for example one containing a hyphen, fails the transformation with the rule named. The reverse strips the prefix, so EnerPlanET's ids return unchanged; a job that references nodes without the prefix is rejected by the reverse rather than guessed at.

docs.title: Field mapping
docs.text: kW→MW means linear with divisor 1000, ×1000 the factor 1000, and inf→absent the absent converter for "inf" with reverse_default: "inf".

docs.title: Payload root
docs.text: EnerPlanET MEME Conversion model_id model.metadata.name copy start_date, end_date model.time.start, model.time.end datetime from 2006-01-02T15:04:05.000Z to RFC 3339 resolution (minutes) model.time.resolution lookup: 15 15min, 30 30min, 60 1H model.metadata.description constant model.carriers.electricity constant {"name": "Electricity", "unit": "MWh"} experiment.mode, .objective, .solver.name, .allow_unmet_demand constants plan, min_cost, highs, {enabled, penalty_price 1e6} user_id, session_id, callback_url, country, lkr none reverse writes "" pypsa none reverse writes EnerPlanET's default line and transformer types custom_demand_time_series, parameters none not carried

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
Each topology[$i] with a to feature becomes model.transmission{${p}_$i} with $p bound to pipe:

EnerPlanET MEME Conversion pipe the key prefix (lv_, mv_) bind from.id, to.id from, to affix prefix n, then match against Calliope's identifier syntax length (km) distance number carrier, bidirectional, capacity constants electricity, true, {"expandable": true}

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
Each topology[$i].from and topology[$i].to becomes model.nodes{n$k} with $k bound to the feature id; a transformer referenced by several connections is written once.

EnerPlanET MEME Conversion id the node key bind geometry.coordinates[0], [1] coords.lon, coords.lat number properties.osm_id name copy properties.demand_energy (kWh/a, when > 0) technologies{demand_$k} with role demand, node n$k, carrier_in electricity, demand_profile in MW ÷ 8 760 000, rounded properties.rated_power (kVA, transformers) trade{grid_$k} with node n$k, import.limit in MW, import.price 300, export kW→MW type, geometry.type, techs, custom_demand_timeseries, properties.id, session_id, created_at, modified_at, f_class_demands, demand_heat none reverse constants: Feature, Point, null, null, the key, "", null, null, null, 0 properties.feature_type, type, f_class, demand_profile, area none reverse: BasePOI, residential, residential, residential, 0 for a node without a grid_* trade; TopologyNode, transformer, null area for one with

residential is EnerPlanET's own fallback when a building has no usage class.

docs.title: Technologies
docs.text:
techs.<key> of a feature becomes technologies{<key>_$k} (or trade{..._$k} for the grid tariffs), with node set to n$k, the feature's node key. The shared rules, applied to every supply technology and the battery:

EnerPlanET (kW, kWh, EUR) MEME (MW, MWh, EUR) Conversion capacity.expandable constant true cont_energy_cap_max capacity.max inf→absent, kW→MW cont_energy_cap_min capacity.min kW→MW cont_energy_cap_max_systemwide capacity.systemwide_max inf→absent, kW→MW cont_lifetime lifetime number cost_interest_rate interest_rate number cost_energy_cap costs.monetary.investment_per_capacity ×1000 cost_om_annual costs.monetary.fixed_om ×1000 cost_om_annual_investment_fraction costs.monetary.fixed_om_fraction 0→absent (MEME allows fixed_om or the fraction, not both); reverse default 0 cost_om_prod costs.monetary.variable_om ×1000 cost_om_con costs.monetary.fuel_cost ×1000 cost_purchase costs.monetary.purchase number

Per technology:

Key MEME Specific fields pv_supply supply, performance physics pv tilt, azimuth, losses→params.tilt, .azimuth, .loss; cont_energy_eff→efficiency; cont_parasitic_eff→native.calliope.flow_out_parasitic_eff battery_storage storage cont_energy_eff→storage.charge_eff and .discharge_eff; cont_storage_cap_max/_min→storage.energy_capacity.max/.min (kWh→MWh, inf→absent); cont_storage_loss→self_discharge; cont_storage_initial→initial_soc; cont_storage_discharge_depth→depth_of_discharge; cost_storage_cap→investment_per_energy_capacity (×1000); energy_capacity.expandable true wind_onshore supply, performance physics wind hub_height, rotor_diameter, nominal_power, turbine_id→params.* biomass_supply, geothermal_supply, water_supply supply shared rules and efficiency only households_supply, non_households_supply trade{households_$k}, trade{non_households_$k} cost_om_con→import.price (×1000); cont_energy_cap_max→import.limit (inf→absent, kW→MW)

docs.title: Not carried
docs.text: PySAM inputs of pv_supply (system_capacity, module_type, inverter_type, optimize_orientation, inv_eff, dc_ac_ratio) and the process parameters of biomass and geothermal exist to generate resource profiles outside the optimiser; MEME has no PySAM, so they have no counterpart. cont_resource_unit, cont_energy_cap_scale, cont_export_cap, cost_export and cont_resource_eff likewise have none. A PV or wind profile must therefore be supplied to MEME separately, as a precomputed series or through TentaCron's resolvents.

docs.title: MEME target compatibility
docs.text:
The produced job passes MEME's decoding and model validation. The per-target gates then apply:

Target Result calliope accepted; warnings that highs is replaced by CBC and that the unmet-demand penalty is approximated by bigM pypsa rejected: PyPSA does not support allow_unmet_demand; remove that constant rule for this target adopt-net0 rejected: AdOpT-NET0 has no transmission mapping in MEME yet

docs.title: The reverse direction
docs.text:
t1k -reverse rebuilds the calculation payload from a job. Everything the tables above mark as a copy or conversion comes back exactly (numbers to their digits, kWh rounded to whole numbers, node ids with their prefix stripped); the reverse constants restore the payload's required keys with the placeholders listed. Three limits:

  • A building without a connection has a node and a demand but no transmission arc, so the reverse has nowhere to place it in topology; it is not restored.
  • user_id, session_id, callback_url, country and lkr are not in a MEME job; the reverse writes empty strings, and the caller must set them (the simulation engine's schema requires a non-empty country).
  • A transformer whose rating is 0 gets no grid trade, and the reverse, which tells transformers from buildings by that trade, restores it as a building.

examples/ holds the payload, the job and the reverse output; pkg/t1k/testdata/ pins both directions, and the tests check that converting the reverse output forward again reproduces the job apart from the standalone building.

docs.title: Adapting the mapping
docs.text: t1k -print-config > my-mapping.json writes the embedded mapping out. Typical edits: change the tariff constants, drop the unmet-demand rule for PyPSA, replace the constant demand by a series (demand_profile naming a model.timeseries entry), or add rules for further building properties. To change the node prefix, edit it in the three places that agree on it: the key template model.nodes{n$k} of the two node rules, the n$k templates of the node references, and the affix prefix of the arc references. t1k -config my-mapping.json runs the edited copy; the configuration reference describes every construct.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
t1k [-config FILE] [-reverse] [-in FILE] [-out FILE] [-compact]
t1k -print-config
t1k -version

The command converts one JSON document with a mapping configuration.

Flag Meaning -config FILE the mapping configuration to apply; without it, the embedded EnerPlanET to MEME mapping is used -in FILE the input document; default: standard input -out FILE the output document; default: standard output -reverse apply the reverse direction: from the target structure back to the source structure -compact write compact JSON; the default is two-space indentation -print-config print the embedded mapping and exit, as a starting point for a custom one (-config is ignored) -version print the version and exit -h, -help print the usage and exit

docs.title: Input and output
docs.text:
• With -in, standard input is not read. With -out, the file is created or overwritten; nothing is written to standard output.
  • The output always ends with a newline, so it can be concatenated or appended to a log.
  • Object keys are written in sorted order, and numbers that were only moved keep their digits (see the evaluation model).

docs.title: Exit status
docs.text:
Status Meaning 0 success 1 the configuration is invalid, the input is not JSON, a rule failed, or a file could not be read or written; the message on standard error says which 2 usage error: an unknown flag or a stray argument; the usage is printed

A failing rule is reported with its position in the configuration, the direction and the path or converter that failed:

t1k: t1k: rule failed: rules[16].rules[5] (forward): length: number: string "far" is not numeric

rules[16].rules[5] is the sixth nested rule of the seventeenth top-level rule. Rules spliced in from a definition carry the definition's name, as in rules[17].rules[0](definitions.feature)[3]: the fourth rule of the definition feature, used by the first nested rule of the eighteenth top-level rule.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# forward and back with the embedded mapping
t1k -in calculation.json -out meme-job.json
t1k -reverse -in meme-job.json -out calculation.json

# a custom mapping in a pipeline
curl -s https://example.invalid/order/17 | t1k -config orders.json -compact | jq .

# start a new mapping from the embedded one
t1k -print-config > my-mapping.json

docs.title: Building
docs.text: make build produces bin/t1k and stamps the version from git describe. A plain go build ./cmd/t1k reports the version as dev; to set it yourself, pass -ldflags "-X main.version=1.2.3".

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: T1K requires Go 1.23 or newer and has no other dependencies.

docs.title: The command
docs.text:
go install github.com/enerplanet/T1K/cmd/t1k@latest
t1k -version

go install places the binary in $(go env GOPATH)/bin; make sure that directory is on your PATH. The command reports the version stamped at build time and dev otherwise; make build in a clone stamps it from git describe (see Command line).

docs.title: The package
docs.text:
go get github.com/enerplanet/T1K/pkg/t1k

import "github.com/enerplanet/T1K/pkg/t1k"

The module path keeps the repository's capitalisation (T1K). The package lives under pkg/t1k, the layout the organisation's shared Go libraries use, and is imported as t1k.

docs.title: From a clone
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/enerplanet/T1K.git
cd T1K
make build        # bin/t1k, version-stamped from git describe
make test         # the test suite
make help         # every target with a description

make lint additionally requires golangci-lint v2. The documentation site requires Python: pip install -r docs/requirements.txt, then make docs serves it with live reload.

docs.title: In a container
docs.text:
The repository's environment/ folder provides a Docker image with the complete toolchain (Go, golangci-lint at the version CI pins, MkDocs) and a compose file whose services run the same Make targets on the bind-mounted checkout. Nothing but Docker and make is needed:

make -C environment build             # one-time image build
make -C environment test  ENV=dev     # go test ./... inside the container
make -C environment check ENV=test    # race tests and lint, as CI runs them
make -C environment docs              # documentation on http://localhost:8000
make -C environment cli ARGS="-in examples/enerplanet-calculation.json -compact"

ENV=dev iterates with Go's caches; ENV=test reproduces CI. The folder's README describes every service and setting.

docs.title: Go package
docs.text:
import "github.com/enerplanet/T1K/pkg/t1k"

API reference: pkg.go.dev/github.com/enerplanet/T1K/pkg/t1k.

docs.title: Transforming
docs.text:
task := t1k.NewTransformTask()
job, err := task.Transform(payload)   // []byte in, []byte out
back, err := task.Reverse(job)

Transform applies the configuration in the forward direction, Reverse in the reverse direction. Both take a JSON document as a byte slice and return one; the output is compact unless WithIndent is set.

A TransformTask binds a configuration and the output format. It holds no per-call state: every call decodes its input, runs on a fresh output document and encodes the result, so one task may be used from several goroutines at once. Creating one task per conversion job, the intended pattern, is cheap: a task is a pointer to a shared, immutable configuration and two formatting options.

docs.title: Configurations
Options
docs.text: Option Effect WithConfig(cfg) use cfg instead of the default; nil keeps the default WithIndent(prefix, indent) indented output, as json.MarshalIndent would produce; empty strings restore compact output

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Every error the package returns wraps one of three sentinels, so callers can classify failures with errors.Is:

Sentinel When ErrConfig the configuration failed to parse or validate, or its file could not be read; the message names the rule and the field ErrInput the document is not valid JSON, or has content after the first document ErrRule a rule could not be applied: a converter received a value it cannot handle, a match guard failed, a bind path is missing from an element, or a variable bound to text is used as an array index; the message names the rule and the direction 
out, err := task.Transform(in)
switch {
case errors.Is(err, t1k.ErrInput):
    // reject the request: the body is not JSON
case errors.Is(err, t1k.ErrRule):
    // the document does not fit the mapping; the message names the rule
}

docs.title: Working with decoded values
docs.text: The package works on JSON text. If a program already holds a decoded value, marshal it first; if it needs the result as a value, unmarshal the output. This keeps the contract small and the number handling explicit: T1K preserves the digits of every number it only moves (1.0 stays 1.0), which a round trip through float64 would not.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This page converts the shipped example in both directions, then writes a small mapping of its own, and ends with the same conversion from Go.

docs.title: Convert the example payload
docs.text:
The repository ships an EnerPlanET calculation payload under examples/. Convert it into a MEME job with the embedded mapping:

t1k -in examples/enerplanet-calculation.json -out meme-job.json

meme-job.json is the body of MEME's POST /simulate. The building and transformer features have become model.nodes (n1, ntrafo_2585, ...), the connections model.transmission arcs (lv_0, mv_2, ...), the annual demands demand_* technologies, the attached PV and battery pv_supply_1 and battery_storage_1, and the transformers model.trade entries that import from the grid. The mapping page explains every field and the identifier scheme.

Convert the job back:

t1k -reverse -in meme-job.json -out calculation.json

calculation.json has the payload's structure again, with EnerPlanET's own ids (1, trafo_2585). Fields a MEME job cannot carry (user_id, callback_url, ...) come back as the placeholders the mapping declares for them; the mapping page lists them.

docs.title: Write your own mapping
docs.text:
Save the following as orders.json:

{
  "name": "orders-to-invoices",
  "rules": [
    {"from": "order.number", "to": "invoice.reference"},
    {"from": "order.total_cents", "to": "invoice.total", "convert": {"linear": {"divisor": 100}}},
    {"from": "order.placed", "to": "invoice.date", "convert": {"datetime": {"from": "RFC3339", "to": "DateOnly"}}},
    {"to": "invoice.currency", "value": "EUR"},
    {
      "each": {"from": "order.lines[$i]", "to": "invoice.items{line_$i}"},
      "rules": [
        {"from": "sku", "to": "article"},
        {"from": "qty", "to": "quantity", "convert": "number"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Run it on an order:

echo '{"order": {"number": "A-17", "total_cents": 1250, "placed": "2026-09-27T10:15:00Z",
       "lines": [{"sku": "bolt", "qty": "40"}, {"sku": "nut", "qty": 40}]}}' \
  | t1k -config orders.json

{
  "invoice": {
    "currency": "EUR",
    "date": "2026-09-27",
    "items": {
      "line_0": {
        "article": "bolt",
        "quantity": 40
      },
      "line_1": {
        "article": "nut",
        "quantity": 40
      }
    },
    "reference": "A-17",
    "total": 12.5
  }
}

The total was divided by 100, the timestamp reduced to a date, the quantity given as text normalised to a number, and the lines keyed by their position. Object keys are written in sorted order; -compact writes the document on one line.

Pipe that output through t1k -config orders.json -reverse and the order comes back:

{
  "order": {
    "lines": [
      {
        "qty": 40,
        "sku": "bolt"
      },
      {
        "qty": 40,
        "sku": "nut"
      }
    ],
    "number": "A-17",
    "placed": "2026-09-27T00:00:00Z",
    "total_cents": 1250
  }
}

The total is in cents again and the items are an array. The date comes back at midnight UTC, because the invoice does not carry the time of day; such losses are the documented exceptions of the reverse direction. currency was a constant for the invoice side only, so the reverse does not write it.

docs.title: Use it from Go
docs.text:
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "os"

    "github.com/enerplanet/T1K/pkg/t1k"
)

func main() {
    payload, err := os.ReadFile("examples/enerplanet-calculation.json")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    task := t1k.NewTransformTask(t1k.WithIndent("", "  "))
    job, err := task.Transform(payload)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(job))
}

See Go package for custom configurations, options and error handling.
